titre: The Domesday Book, the Inventory of Norman England (1086)
accroche: At Christmas 1085, William the Conqueror demands an inventory so precise that not a single ox, cow, or pig escapes it.
contenu_vulgarise:
At Christmas 1085, 19 years after conquering England at Hastings, William the Conqueror gathers his council at Gloucester. He wants to know, county by county, who owns what, what it is worth, and how much tax he can draw from it. The order goes out at once: royal commissioners will travel the kingdom to record everything. The result, completed in record time for the era, will become the oldest administrative document preserved by the English state: the Domesday Book.

## A Sworn Inquiry, County by County

The commissioners do not merely observe: in each county seat, they summon the sheriff, the barons, and their vassals, and put a fixed list of questions to sworn local jurors: who held the land before 1066, who holds it now, what it is worth, how many animals, mills, and serfs it has. Each answer is cross-checked against that of a neighboring jury, to limit lying. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, written the same year by a monk of Peterborough, is indignant at this thoroughness: “there was not a single hide nor a single yard of land, nor even — it is shameful to tell, though he was not ashamed to do it — an ox, a cow, or a pig that was not set down in his account.” The name “Domesday” comes from this: a century later, the royal treasurer Richard FitzNeal will explain that the kingdom nicknamed it that because, like the Last Judgment, its verdict allows no appeal.

## A Project Its Commissioner Did Not Live to See Finished

The inquiry itself moves fast: most of the answers are gathered in a few months of 1086. But the work of putting it into shape (copying, abridging, and sorting thousands of local statements into bound volumes) takes longer than the textbook account suggests. Little Domesday, the volume covering East Anglia, remains in its raw state: more detailed than the rest, never reduced or fair-copied, like a draft that no one had time to polish. William dies in September 1087, less than two years after launching the inquiry, and historians spot in the finished pages the signs of work done under pressure and then abruptly halted. Some, such as David Roffe, even argue that the inquiry and the writing of the book were two distinct undertakings, the second perhaps continuing after the king's death. The object presented as proof of a relentless Norman administration is thus, in part, a project left open: the trace of a power that wanted to know everything faster than it could write everything down.

citation.texte: The kingdom calls it “Domesday,” the Day of Judgment — for just as no subterfuge can escape the verdict of that final and dreadful trial, so its word can be neither denied nor set aside without penalty, once it has been invoked.
citation.source: *Dialogus de Scaccario* (Dialogue of the Exchequer), c. 1179

carte.punch: William wanted to know everything: not an ox, a cow, or a pig escaped him.
carte.idee: In 1085, William the Conqueror orders a survey of England so meticulous that nothing escapes it. Its name, “Domesday,” comes from a verdict with no appeal, but the book itself remained, in part, an unfinished project at the king's death.

quiz.question: Why does the Domesday Book bear the name of the Last Judgment?
choix: Because it was completed on the day of a major religious feast
Because its verdict on a piece of land allows no appeal
Because it recorded only lands belonging to the Church
Because William had it written on his deathbed, in 1087
quiz.explication: The royal treasurer Richard FitzNeal explains it in his *Dialogus de Scaccario* (Dialogue of the Exchequer): like the Last Judgment, the book's verdict on a piece of land allows no appeal, nothing to do with a religious feast, an inventory limited to Church lands, or a last-minute writing.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the royal commissioners limit false testimony in the inquiry?
choix: By cross-checking each answer against that of a neighboring jury
By sending two independent commissioners to each county
By requiring the sheriff to sign each statement personally
By comparing the statements with earlier Norman tax records
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Each answer from a sworn local jury was cross-checked against that of a neighboring jury, to limit lying in the statements.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What distinguishes Little Domesday, the volume on East Anglia, from the rest of the Domesday Book?
choix: It was written in Norman French rather than Latin
It covers only lands belonging to the Church
It remains in its raw state, more detailed, never fair-copied
It was lost, then found again in the 19th century
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Unlike the rest of the Domesday Book, Little Domesday, more detailed, was never abridged or fair-copied.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the historian David Roffe suggest about the Domesday Book?
choix: That the name “Domesday” appears in no medieval source
That the commissioners exaggerated the value of the lands to flatter the king
That the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle invented the anecdote about the oxen and cows
That the inquiry and the writing of the book were two distinct undertakings
quiz_supplementaire.explication: David Roffe argues that the inquiry carried out in 1086 and the writing of the book were two distinct undertakings, the second perhaps continuing after William's death.
